#487. NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement

How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace.

NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs.

“We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.”

Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000.

“Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”

Building on two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, GRACE will use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs.

“GRACE Aerospace is thankful and honored to participate in the program,” said Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace. “We look forward to growing and learning from industry experts and supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority.”

NASA’s enhanced supplier program is part of the agency’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.

#486. Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

"It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," says Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system."

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

At its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a new cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

(A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.)

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues

Piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," says Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

The disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts new light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

"It actually was happening," Young says. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence."

However, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

The consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young says.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

The findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," says Young.

#485. New York is banning AI chatbot toys for kids. Heres what the law covers.

Talking dolls and stuffed animals have been holiday gifts for decades. But with the rapid adoption of AI across all industries, many of the toys on shelves today can answer questions, make up stories, and carry on full conversations with a child.

In New York, those toys have a few more months on the shelves. On Tuesday, Nov. 24, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of children’s toys with built-in AI companions in the state for five years. The ban takes effect Feb. 22, 2027, though, so the toys can still be sold over the holidays.

A toy has to meet two definitions to fall under the ban, the first being who the toy is made for. New York borrows a federal definition that covers products designed or intended for play by kids 12 and younger. The age printed on the box is one factor, alongside how the toy is packaged and advertised and who shoppers generally understand it to be for. That means a "13+" label alone wouldn’t settle whether a toy is covered.

The second definition is about what the toy does. New York defines an AI companion as a system designed to mimic an ongoing relationship: It remembers past conversations and preferences to personalize its responses, asks about feelings unprompted, and keeps conversations going about personal topics. A doll that simply plays a few prerecorded phrases falls outside that definition.

The state attorney general can seek civil penalties of up to $15,000 a day for each violation. Yikes!

Over the past year, researchers and child advocates have raised concerns about what AI toys might say to kids, what information they collect about them, and how they encourage children to see a chatbot as a friend. Some toys did better than in previous tests; for example, FoloToy's Kumma teddy bear, which discussed sexual topics in last year's tests, shut down age-inappropriate prompts this year.

#484. Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years

Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."

Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve."

"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said.

He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also said Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.

Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the company sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.

He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.

"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he said.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

#482. 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship."

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions."

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax

The team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

One sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

The addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past

The sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

The pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an important maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

The new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

The findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical."

#480. Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island

New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

In the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in New Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

Resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of New Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”

So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park. This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, shows the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

The uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

In 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.

#477. Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions."

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

#476. What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?

Hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.

Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.

A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.

In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.

Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.

The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory

Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.

According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.

Astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.

The new paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.

One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.

A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.

Marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.

This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.

What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks

The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.

Although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.

This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.

Marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.

The researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.

Marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.

However, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.

While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.

Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

#475. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 26, 2026

The Moon is still looking almost full tonight, despite being a couple of days past the Full Moon. It's now in its Waning Gibbous phase, meaning the illuminated portion we can see is gradually getting smaller each night.

As of Thursday, Nov. 26, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Gibbous phase, with 96% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Serenitatis, Kepler Crater, as well as the Tycho Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Gassendi Crater, the Endymion Crater, and the Posidonius Crater. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 14 and 15 landing spots, plus the Descartes Highlands.

In North America, the next Full Moon will take place on December 23. In other time zones it will fall on December 24.

It takes around 29.5 days for the Moon to move through all its phases, according to NASA. Throughout this period, the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun determines how much of its illuminated surface we can see. Starting with a New Moon, the visible portion gradually increases until it reaches a Full Moon, before shrinking again as the cycle comes back around.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#474. Shivelyuch Socked In

A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.

In the same way that Shivelyuch (also called Shiveluch) frequently displays volcanic activity, it is also chronically obscured by clouds. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes.

The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome, formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows.

In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months, according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano.

On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft. In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports, prompting the cancellation of multiple flights.

#472. Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

Physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

The achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

By measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

The research was published in Physical Review Letters.

"Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out."

Gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

Searching for Cracks in the Standard Model

The Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Despite those successes, the theory remains incomplete. One of its most significant shortcomings is its inability to explain the overwhelming abundance of matter compared with antimatter in the observable universe.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere -- or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that's a pretty big loophole. We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer."

Gabrielse has devoted decades of his scientific career to investigating this mystery. His research group previously developed methods for isolating individual electrons and determining their magnetic properties with exceptional precision.

He also helped establish the field of low-energy antimatter research by pioneering techniques for slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons. The latest achievement combines these two areas of expertise, extending the sophisticated quantum control previously demonstrated with electrons to an individual antimatter particle.

Almost everything on Earth is composed of three familiar particles: electrons, protons, and neutrons. A universe made of antimatter could contain their respective counterparts: positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. According to Gabrielse, if everything on Earth were constructed from antimatter instead of ordinary matter, distinguishing between the two would be remarkably difficult.

The dramatic differences emerge when matter and antimatter come into contact. An electron and a positron, for example, can annihilate when they encounter one another. This makes storing antimatter particularly challenging, as contact with the material walls of an ordinary container would almost certainly destroy the trapped particle.

"If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully," Gabrielse said. "To be clear, it's not dangerous. We don't have enough antimatter to make an explosion."

To overcome this problem, the Northwestern researchers employed an advanced particle trap that uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields. These fields keep the positron suspended in an empty region of space, preventing it from coming into contact with the surrounding material.

By effectively creating a container that does not require the particle to touch any physical walls, the team has managed to keep a single positron confined in Gabrielse's laboratory for months.

Capturing a positron presents another considerable technical hurdle. Certain atomic nuclei release positrons as they undergo radioactive decay. For their experiment, the researchers used sodium-22, a rare radioactive isotope of sodium. Positrons emitted during this process initially carry tremendous amounts of energy.

The physicists substantially reduced the particle's speed before directing it into the trap's near-perfect vacuum. Inside, the temperature is maintained at approximately 300 millikelvins, equivalent to just 0.3 degrees above absolute zero.

Under these extremely cold conditions, the positron can settle into its lowest possible quantum energy state.

"We cool it down so much that it's in its quantum ground state," Gabrielse said. "We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time."

Putting Matter and Antimatter to the Ultimate Test

Beyond capturing and cooling the positron, the researchers demonstrated that they could deliberately change its individual quantum energy states and detect those changes.

Using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, the physicists transferred carefully controlled amounts of energy to the particle and observed the resulting transitions between quantum states. This ability is crucial to their larger objective of determining the positron's magnetic properties with exceptional accuracy and comparing them directly with those of an electron.

In earlier research, Gabrielse and his colleagues used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to determine the electron's magnetic moment, a measure of its magnetic properties, with a precision of approximately one part in 10 trillion. That achievement ranks among the most precise measurements ever performed on an elementary particle.

The team now intends to conduct an equivalent measurement using the trapped positron. Comparing the two results could provide an extraordinarily sensitive test of current particle physics theories and potentially uncover evidence of previously unknown physics.

"Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements," Gabrielse said. "If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century."

The study, "One-positron quantum cyclotron," received support from the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565).

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was returned to the job earlier this week, the board reinstating him amidst plummeting stock prices and apparent intervention from President Donald Trump. Now doubt is being cast on allegations that one of Huang's affair partners was a Chinese spy.

Huang has admitted to cheating on his wife with at least four partners as of this week, however his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) has drawn the most scrutiny. A former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, Ms. Huang is suspected of being an intelligent agent who shared information with the Chinese government and smuggled Nvidia chips into China, circumventing U.S. restrictions.

As such, Nvidia opened an independent investigation once Huang and Ms. Huang's relationship came to light, as well as established a committee to oversee the company's national security policies and export control compliance. Huang will also be interviewed by the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Select Committee on China, and House Intelligence Committee on Dec. 1, and testify before the U.S. Senate on Dec. 3.

Instead, current evidence indicates that the pair's extramarital entanglement may have been a matter of ordinary human infidelity rather than deliberate international espionage. U.S officials reportedly informed congressional staffers of this in a briefing on Nov. 24, the day after Nvidia reinstated Huang. #469. A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has made an unexpected discovery in our own solar system. Images captured between September 16 and 24, 2026, revealed a previously unknown comet, the first discovered by the mission.

The achievement is particularly remarkable given that Euclid was built to capture detailed images of distant galaxies rather than track rapidly moving objects such as comets. The speed with which researchers identified and confirmed the discovery demonstrates that Euclid can detect new comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun. This capability could eventually help identify a target for ESA's upcoming Comet Interceptor mission.

Mikko Pöntinen, a PhD student at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium. Pöntinen developed specialized software to detect and track small solar system objects appearing in the telescope's images.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images -- the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas."

The object appeared in a region of the sky known as the 'Euclid Deep Field North'. Over several days, the telescope captured it in five separate fields of view, taking between two and four exposures of each field for a total of 16 exposures.

After searching catalogs of known asteroids and comets without finding a match, Pöntinen submitted the observations to the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) as a potential new comet. The report enabled astronomers using telescopes on Earth to carry out additional observations. On October 8, the MPC officially confirmed the discovery. The comet has been designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

The newly discovered comet is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (about 800 million miles) from Earth. That distance is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point somewhere between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

However, the comet is traveling well outside the relatively flat plane in which the planets orbit the Sun. It is currently positioned almost directly above the Sun, following a sweeping path over the solar system that will take thousands of years to complete.

The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center (MPC) serves as the central international hub for observations of asteroids and comets. It gathers data from observers around the world to verify discoveries, determine orbital paths, and assign official designations. As additional observations become available, astronomers will be able to calculate the orbital period of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) more precisely.

Although Euclid has spotted comets before, all of them had already been discovered. Several aspects of the telescope's design and observing strategy make finding previously unknown objects within our solar system especially difficult.

Euclid intentionally avoids the region of the sky surrounding the plane of the solar system, where large numbers of asteroids and comets can be found. Dust concentrated in this region produces unwanted light that could interfere with the telescope's sensitive observations of the distant universe.

The spacecraft also follows a 'step-and-stare' observing strategy, typically imaging each section of the sky only once. This means researchers cannot readily direct Euclid back toward a newly detected comet to gather more information about it.

Identifying objects within our solar system is nevertheless an important part of Euclid's scientific work. Researchers must account for everything appearing in its images so that unrelated features, including comet trails and unwanted light, can be removed without compromising the accuracy of its galaxy measurements.

"Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet's orbit and Euclid's scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images," says Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist, and part of the discovery team.

Euclid's unexpected discovery also provides valuable experience for scientists working on ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission. Although the newly identified comet is not an appropriate destination for the spacecraft, the successful detection and rapid notification process demonstrates how the two missions could work together to identify potential targets.

"While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are of course happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on," adds Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

Comets are ancient bodies composed of ice and dust that remain from the formation of our solar system approximately 4.6 billion years ago. Most originate in the distant Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, regions located beyond the orbits of the outer planets (interstellar comets come from other solar systems).

As a comet approaches the Sun, increasing temperatures cause its ice to turn directly into gas. Escaping gas and dust form a glowing, fuzzy cloud known as a 'coma,' as well as an extended tail.

Because comets native to our solar system have remained relatively unchanged since their formation, they preserve valuable evidence of the materials and environmental conditions that existed when the planets were taking shape. Studying these ancient objects may also help scientists understand the origins of Earth's water and the chemical building blocks of life.

Euclid's Hunt for Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The primary goal of the Euclid mission is to uncover how dark matter and dark energy influence the visible universe. During its six-year survey, the space telescope will examine the shapes and movements of billions of galaxies at distances reaching up to 10 billion light-years.

The comet discovery was reported on behalf of the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium by M. Pöntinen, A. A. Nucita, A. Franco, M. Granvik, B. Altieri, S. Kruk, B. Y. Irureta-Goyena and B. Carry.

#467. U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.

"The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles."

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."

CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response."

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

#465. Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds

Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago.

Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant barrier for plants, animals, and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams”.

In contrast, the Mirning People of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have lived for tens of thousands of years on this southern margin. They have watched the landscapes change and sea levels fall and rise with the build-up and collapse of the last ice age about 20,000 years ago.

To an untrained eye the Nullarbor Plain appears deceptively simple and featureless. However, beneath the immense plain lies a remarkable, largely hidden underground world.

Over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone and created complex cave networks that can extend for kilometers underground. Sadly, the caves remain poorly understood, partly because they’re only really known and accessible where they breach the surface.

Our new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, reveals a new way to track these cave systems even when they are deeply buried. Our work helps explain the formation of previously mysterious, shallow trench features on the Nullarbor. It also provides a new way to identify hidden caves elsewhere – even beyond our own planet.

Scattered across the Nullarbor are tell-tale signs of its vulnerability to being dissolved – small cave openings and shallow depressions.

But there are also structures of previously unknown origin and significance: long (up to 20 km), shallow (a few meters) trenches that trend roughly north-south. They’re almost invisible from the ground, but we can clearly see them in modern digital landscape models.

These shallow trenches look somewhat like flat-bottomed valleys, but they were not carved by rivers. They begin and end abruptly and are not connected to existing rivers or drainage networks that extend into the upland areas around the Nullarbor.

They also lack typical river branching patterns and the sediments within them don’t show any evidence of being deposited from flowing water.

To understand how these strange structures formed, we combined several investigative techniques.

First, we mapped the trenches using drone and aerial photography, as well as detailed satellite-based digital landscape models. Then the layers of soil and rock were measured in boreholes and caves.

Finally, we used specialized geophysical techniques to “see” inside the Earth, somewhat similar to the way an X-ray enables us to see our internal body structures from the outside.

The work demonstrated that the shallow surface trenches sit above deep zones of broken rock, and in places line up with known cave systems and sinkholes.

This means the trenches are mere muted surface expressions of deeply buried cave systems. These systems are slowly, over millions of years, “collapsing upwards” through the overlying rock layers to reach the surface.

The results of this work will change how scientists interpret cave landscapes globally. It shows that to explain the surface structures we see, we must look deeper than we might think.

Understanding where voids may exist underground can be important for planning both surface (buildings, roads) and subsurface (tunnels, sewers) engineering works, mitigating geological hazards, and accessing and protecting groundwater resources.

Pockmarked karst landscapes (where rocks are dissolved by water, resulting in caves and sinkholes) represent 15% of the ice-free Earth’s surface and supply water to 10–25% of the global population.

More fundamentally, caves are important scientific archives. Because caves are sheltered from surface weathering and erosion processes, they can preserve snapshots of ancient environments and ecosystems that would otherwise be lost to time.

Furthermore, they may host an array of strange and vulnerable life-forms that have evolved and adapted in isolation. These are some of the least studied organisms on Earth.

To learn more, we must first locate the cave structures. And the results of our study could be very important in this regard.

The implications of this new work even extend beyond our own planet. Because caves offer a stable environment and shelter from damaging space radiation, they provide promising exploration sites for life on other planets.

Mapping of planetary surfaces within our Solar System has identified numerous potential caves, including some thought to be related to karst on Mars.

The Nullarbor’s dry, stable surface is an excellent analogue to help locate the subtle surface fingerprints of hidden cave systems on planets that now lack a dynamic water-cycle – such as Mars. Even if the caves are barren of life, they could be attractive bases for future human explorers.

How many other apparently simple landscapes around the world or on other planets are concealing large cave systems underneath? We don’t yet know, but the trenches we studied are unlikely to be unique. Similar subtle landforms are likely to have been overlooked elsewhere, too.

Sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting in understated but plain view, in landscapes we think we already understand.

The authors would like to acknowledge Matthias Leopold from The University of Western Australia; Rok Ciglič, Mateja Ferk, Jure Tičar, Matija Zorn and Matej Jelovčan from the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts (ZRC SAZU); John A. Webb from La Trobe University; Uroš Stepišnik, Matej Dolenec, Primož Miklavc, Tomislav Popit and Andrej Šmuc from the University of Ljubljana; and Jian-xin Zhao from The University of Queensland.
